% ============================================================================
\section{Task 2A: Software Prefetching (5 points)}
% ============================================================================

\subsection{Overview}

Software prefetching issues explicit cache-line fetch instructions ahead of demand loads,
hiding memory latency by overlapping data transfer with computation.
We implement the prefetch stage as a \textbf{scalar} (non-SIMD) kernel with five prefetch modes,
controlled by compile-time defines:

\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{Mode 0 (none)}: baseline: no prefetch instructions.
    \item \textbf{Mode 1 (within\_row)}: prefetches $A$ and $B$ elements \texttt{PF\_DIST} floats ahead within the current dot-product loop, once per cache line (every 16 floats).
    \item \textbf{Mode 2 (next\_B)}: prefetches the start of the \emph{next} $B$ row before computing the current dot product, so the next column's data is already in cache.
    \item \textbf{Mode 3 (C\_output)}: prefetches the $C$ output location before the dot product.
    \item \textbf{Mode 4 (all)}: combines modes 1, 2, and 3.
\end{itemize}

Two parameters are tuned:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{Prefetch distance (\texttt{PF\_DIST})}: how many floats ahead to prefetch (0, 16, 32, 64, 128).
    \item \textbf{Cache fill level (\texttt{PF\_HINT})}: \texttt{\_MM\_HINT\_T0} (L1), \texttt{T1} (L2), \texttt{T2} (L3), \texttt{NTA} (non-temporal).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Impact of Matrix Size}

\midrule

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

All measurements in this section were collected with \textbf{hardware prefetchers disabled}
(MSR \texttt{0x1A4} = \texttt{0xF}) to isolate the effect of software prefetching alone.

Software prefetching provides only marginal benefit on this scalar kernel (${<}1.07{\times}$ at all sizes).
The scalar triple loop is \emph{compute-bound}: each output element requires $K$ multiply-accumulate iterations processed one float at a time, and the CPU's out-of-order engine can overlap demand misses with the long instruction stream.
Adding explicit prefetch instructions introduces overhead (extra $\mu$ops competing for execution ports) that nearly cancels any latency-hiding benefit.

\subsection{CPU Metrics Analysis}

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{../plots/prefetch_cache_misses.png}
\caption{L1-D, L2, and LLC misses: no prefetch vs.\ next\_B mode (T0, distances 64 and 128)}
\end{figure}

Key observations from the cache miss data:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{L1-D misses decrease slightly} with next\_B prefetching (e.g.\ at 1024: 732M $\rightarrow$ 690M for dist=128), because the prefetch pulls the next $B$ row into L1 before demand.
    \item \textbf{L2 misses are unchanged} (${\sim}745$M at 1024) because the working set far exceeds L2 regardless of prefetching.
    \item \textbf{LLC misses are similar} across configurations, confirming that the bottleneck is DRAM bandwidth, not cache miss latency.
    \item \textbf{Within-row prefetching (mode 1) increases instruction count dramatically} (681M+ \texttt{sw\_prefetch\_access} at 1024) without reducing misses, because the prefetch instructions consume execution-port bandwidth that the compute loop needs.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Execution Time and Speedup}

\subsubsection{Speedup by Prefetch Mode}

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth]{../plots/prefetch_mode_comparison.png}
\caption{Best speedup per prefetch mode across matrix sizes}
\end{figure}

\textbf{next\_B} is the only mode that achieves speedup ${\geq}1.0{\times}$ at every size (best configs 1.01--1.07$\times$).
\textbf{within\_row} and \textbf{all} lose even at their \emph{best} configurations for sizes up to 1024 (0.73--0.94$\times$), and their typical configurations are far worse (0.42--0.82$\times$ with T0, collapsing to 0.13--0.17$\times$ with NTA): a prefetch every 16 iterations of the inner $K$ loop adds instruction overhead that overwhelms any benefit.
At 2048 their best configs scrape just past parity (1.03$\times$ and 1.10$\times$), which is within the naive baseline's run-to-run variance.
\textbf{C\_output} is neutral: the single output store per dot product is too infrequent to benefit from prefetching.

\subsubsection{Speedup by Prefetch Distance}

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.8\textwidth]{../plots/prefetch_distance_speedup.png}
\caption{Speedup vs.\ prefetch distance for next\_B mode (T0 hint)}
\end{figure}

The optimal prefetch distance is \textbf{64--128 floats} (4--8 cache lines ahead).
At distance 0, the prefetch fires too late to hide any latency.
At distances 16--128, the small improvement (${\sim}1.02$--$1.05{\times}$) is consistent across sizes, with 128 slightly better at large matrices where the next $B$ row is more likely to be evicted.

\subsubsection{Speedup by Cache Fill Level}

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering

\caption{Speedup vs.\ matrix size for different cache fill levels (next\_B mode)}
\end{figure}

\textbf{T0} (prefetch into L1) is the best hint for next\_B mode.
T1 and T2 are slightly worse because prefetching into L2/L3 still requires a demand miss to pull the line into L1 when the dot product actually uses it.
NTA (non-temporal) performs similarly to T0 at large sizes but offers no advantage.

\subsection{Optimal Parameters}

\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{Best prefetch mode}: next\_B (mode 2): prefetch the start of the next $B$ row.
    \item \textbf{Best prefetch distance}: 64--128 floats.
    \item \textbf{Best cache fill level}: \texttt{\_MM\_HINT\_T0} (L1).
\end{itemize}

However, even the best configuration achieves only ${\sim}1.03$--$1.06{\times}$ speedup, even with hardware prefetchers disabled.
The scalar kernel is compute-bound: the CPU spends most cycles retiring scalar multiply-accumulate instructions, not stalling on cache misses, so there is little memory latency for software prefetching to hide.

\subsection{Effect of Hardware Prefetchers}

with all four hardware prefetchers enabled (MSR \texttt{0x1A4 = 0x0}) and disabled
(MSR \texttt{0x1A4 = 0xF}) across five matrix sizes.

Size & ON & OFF & ON & OFF & ON & OFF & ON & OFF & ON & OFF \\

2048 & 5{,}217 & 9{,}418 &  3.29 &  1.82 &   218.4M & 5{,}897M & 6{,}250M & 6{,}030M &   33.9M & 1{,}188M \\

\end{tabular}
\end{table}

At small sizes (128--256), the naive kernel is actually \emph{faster} with hardware
prefetchers \textbf{off}.  At these sizes the whole working set fits in L2/L3, so an
L1 miss costs almost nothing: there is no memory latency for the prefetchers to hide.
They still fetch speculatively, however, and this useless extra traffic (visible as
\emph{higher} L2 misses with prefetchers on: 84K vs.\ 52K at $128$) gets in the way of
the real loads.  The runs are also very short (1--17\,ms), so part of the gap is simply
measurement noise.  The prefetchers only start to matter at size $2048$, below.

At size 512--1024, the two configurations are nearly identical (${\sim}4.4$--$4.6$ GFLOP/s),
since the working set spans L2 and the hardware prefetcher's benefit roughly cancels
its overhead.

The hardware prefetcher becomes essential at \textbf{size 2048}: with prefetchers on,
the naive kernel achieves 3.29 GFLOP/s in 5.2 seconds; with prefetchers off, it drops
to 1.82 GFLOP/s and takes 9.4 seconds, a $1.81{\times}$ slowdown.
LLC misses explode from 34M to 1.19B without prefetching, confirming that at this size
the working set far exceeds L3 and the hardware streamer is critical for maintaining
any memory-level parallelism.

\subsection{Analysis Questions}

\subsubsection{Q1: Speedup Trend with Matrix Size}

Prefetch speedup is nearly flat across matrix sizes, staying in the $1.00$--$1.06{\times}$ range for the best mode (next\_B), even with hardware prefetchers disabled.
The scalar kernel is compute-bound at all sizes: at small sizes the data fits in cache so there are few misses to hide; at large sizes the out-of-order engine overlaps the long scalar instruction stream with demand misses, leaving little exposed latency for software prefetch to cover.

\subsubsection{Q2: Best Prefetch Distance}

The best prefetch distance is \textbf{64--128 floats} (256--512 bytes, or 4--8 cache lines).
This is enough lead time for the prefetch to complete before the demand load, without being so far ahead that the prefetched line is evicted before use.
At distance 0, the prefetch is useless (the demand load fires simultaneously).
Distances 16--32 are marginally worse because the prefetch may not complete in time for the next iteration.

\subsubsection{Q3: Best Cache Fill Level}

\textbf{T0} (\texttt{\_MM\_HINT\_T0}, prefetch into L1) achieves the maximum speedup.
This makes sense because the dot-product loop immediately reads the prefetched data, so placing it in L1 avoids one additional cache-to-cache transfer.
T1/T2 prefetch into L2/L3, requiring a subsequent L1 miss on the demand load, which partially negates the latency hiding.
NTA is designed for streaming data that won't be reused, but each $B$ row is accessed only once per $C$ element anyway, so NTA offers no structural advantage here.

% ============================================================================
\section{Task 2B: SIMD (1 point)}
% ============================================================================

\subsection{SIMD Implementation}

The SGEMM kernel uses a \textbf{register-tiled vectorized dot product} approach.
The matrix layout stores both $A$ and $B$ with the reduction axis $K$ as the contiguous (unit-stride) dimension: $C[i][j] = \sum_p A[i][p] \cdot B[j][p]$.
This means the natural SIMD strategy is to vectorize the dot product over $p$.

The micro-kernel computes a $4 \times 2$ block of $C$ at once using 8 independent \texttt{\_\_m256} accumulators:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item For each step along $K$, two \texttt{\_mm256\_loadu\_ps} loads fetch 8 elements from two rows of $B$.
    \item Four \texttt{\_mm256\_broadcast\_ss} calls broadcast one element from each of four $A$ rows.
    \item Eight \texttt{\_mm256\_fmadd\_ps} instructions accumulate all $4 \times 2 = 8$ partial-product vectors.
\end{itemize}
This yields 8 FMAs per step from only 6 loads, and the 8 independent accumulator chains saturate the FMA pipeline (FMA latency ${\sim}4$ cycles, throughput $2$/cycle, requiring ${\geq}8$ independent chains).
After the $K$ loop, each accumulator is horizontally reduced (\texttt{hsum256}) to a single scalar, stored into the corresponding $C[i][j]$.

Leftover rows ($M \bmod 4$), columns ($N \bmod 2$), and $K$ elements ($K \bmod 8$) fall to a scalar cleanup path.

Two SIMD widths were benchmarked:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{SSE 128-bit}: 4 floats per vector, $4 \times 2$ register tile, 8 accumulators
    \item \textbf{AVX2 256-bit}: 8 floats per vector, $4 \times 2$ register tile, 8 accumulators
\end{itemize}
None of these include cache blocking: the kernel streams through $A$ and $B$ from whatever cache level holds them.

\textbf{Instruction count observation:} SIMD does \emph{not} significantly reduce instruction count: the SIMD versions issue roughly the same number of instructions as the naive version (within ${\sim}7\%$).
This is because the register-tiled micro-kernel still executes $O(MNK)$ FMA instructions; SIMD packs 4/8/16 multiply-adds into each instruction but also adds overhead from broadcasts, horizontal reductions, and cleanup.
The speedup comes not from fewer instructions but from each instruction doing $4{\times}$/$8{\times}$/$16{\times}$ more work.

\subsection{Analysis Questions}

\subsubsection{Q1: Speedup Trends}

Two trends are visible:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Wider SIMD $\Rightarrow$ higher peak speedup.}
    AVX2 reaches \simdWidthAVXFtwelveSpeedup{} at $512{\times}512$ while SSE reaches \simdWidthSSEFtwelveSpeedup{}.
    The ratio roughly tracks the $2{\times}$ vector width difference but falls short of
    the theoretical $2{\times}$ due to load/broadcast overhead and the horizontal reduction.

    \item \textbf{Speedup rises then falls with matrix size.}
    At small sizes (128) the loop overhead and scalar cleanup dominate, limiting SSE to \simdWidthSSEOhtwentyeightSpeedup{}.
    Peak is around $512$--$1024$, where the working set fits mostly in L2 and the micro-kernel runs at near-peak throughput.
    At $2048$ both widths drop significantly (AVX2 falls from \simdWidthAVXTtwentyfourSpeedup{} to \simdWidthAVXTfortyeightSpeedup{}) because the $A$ and $B$ matrices no longer fit in L2, and the unblocked kernel becomes memory-bound.
    Notably, AVX2 (\simdWidthAVXTfortyeightGflops{} GFLOP/s) drops below SSE (\simdWidthSSETfortyeightGflops{} GFLOP/s) at $2048$: the wider vectors require more data per instruction, making the memory bottleneck worse.
\end{enumerate}

\subsubsection{Q2: Best SIMD Width}

\textbf{AVX2 (256-bit)} achieves the maximum speedup at sizes up to $1024$, peaking at
\simdWidthAVXTtwentyfourSpeedup{} at $1024{\times}1024$ (\simdWidthAVXTtwentyfourGflops{} GFLOP/s).
Each 256-bit FMA processes 8 floats, double SSE's 4, so the arithmetic throughput roughly doubles
while instruction-issue overhead stays constant.

However, at $2048{\times}2048$ AVX2 (\simdWidthAVXTfortyeightGflops{} GFLOP/s) actually falls
below SSE (\simdWidthSSETfortyeightGflops{} GFLOP/s) because the wider vectors demand more
memory bandwidth per instruction, and the unblocked kernel is fully memory-bound at this size.
Cache blocking (Task 2C) is required to sustain AVX2's throughput advantage at large sizes.

% ============================================================================
\section{Task 2C: Software Prefetching + SIMD (3 points)}
% ============================================================================

\subsection{Combined Implementation}

The combined kernel (\texttt{matmul\_optimized.cpp}) layers three techniques on top of the Stage-1 SIMD micro-kernel:

\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{6$\times$16 AVX2 micro-kernel.} Each output tile spans 6 rows of $C$ and 16 contiguous columns, held in 12 \texttt{\_\_m256} accumulators (two per row: \texttt{c0l}/\texttt{c0h} through \texttt{c5l}/\texttt{c5h}).
    Per $K$ step: 2 packed-$B$ loads + 6 $A$ broadcasts $\rightarrow$ 12 FMAs.
    The 12 independent chains hide FMA latency and keep the pipeline saturated.

    \item \textbf{B-panel packing.} $B$ is stored column-major (K contiguous per column), so loading 16 columns at position $p$ would be strided.
    Before each $NC$-column block, $B$ is packed into a scratch buffer $\texttt{Bpack}[p][j]$ so that the micro-kernel's $B$ loads are unit-stride.

    \item \textbf{Cache blocking.} The output is traversed in $MC{\times}NC$ blocks (default $MC{=}96$, $NC{=}64$) with loop order $jc \rightarrow ic \rightarrow jr \rightarrow ir$.
    The packed $B$ panel ($K \times NC$ floats) is reused across all $MC$ rows, and each $A$ sub-panel ($MC \times K$) is reused across all $NC$ columns, so both stay resident in L2.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Software Prefetch in the Combined Kernel}

The combined kernel deliberately ships \emph{without} software prefetch. This was a
measured decision, not an omission. We added \texttt{\_mm\_prefetch} on the packed-$B$
stream (distance and fill level as compile-time knobs, default 64 floats ahead, T0) and
compared against the identical kernel without it, interleaved back-to-back on a pinned
core so thermal drift affects both variants equally
(variants preserved in \texttt{bench/experiments/}):

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Software prefetch on the combined kernel, \texttt{optimized} stage, $1024^3$ (ms)}
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
Variant & Times (interleaved) & Mean \\
\midrule
No prefetch                & 22.7 / 22.3 / 21.4 & $\sim$22.1 \\
$B$-stream prefetch        & 23.3 / 22.4 / 23.8 & $\sim$23.2 \\
$B$ + all six $A$ streams  & 26.2 -- 31.3       & $\sim$28 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Prefetching is 0--5\% \emph{slower} on the $B$ stream and $\sim$25\% slower when the six
$A$ broadcast streams are prefetched as well. The mechanism: packing already converts
every inner-loop access into a unit-stride walk, which the L2 hardware streamer predicts
perfectly, so the software hint adds no information; it only spends load-port slots
that the 12-FMA-per-8-load inner loop cannot spare. This is consistent with the flat
distance curve in the standalone prefetch stage (Task 2A).

\subsection{Software Prefetch on the Unblocked SIMD Kernel}

To confirm that this null result is a property of the \emph{blocked, packed} kernel and
not of software prefetch itself, we ran the same experiment on the Stage-1 SIMD kernel,
which has no cache blocking (prefetch on its two $B$ streams, 64 floats ahead, T0):

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Prefetch on the unblocked SIMD kernel, \texttt{simd} stage times (ms), interleaved}
\begin{tabular}{lrrl}
\toprule
Size & Without & With & Verdict \\
\midrule
$128^3$  & 0.047--0.050 & 0.054--0.058 & $\sim$15\% slower \\
$256^3$  & 0.380        & 0.430--0.437 & $\sim$13\% slower \\
$512^3$  & 2.98--3.01   & 3.30--3.46   & $\sim$12\% slower \\
$1024^3$ & 26.3--26.6   & 28.3--29.5   & $\sim$9\% slower \\
$1536^3$ & 132.2 / 132.5 & 157.3 / 127.4 & wash (transition) \\
$2048^3$ & 366--464 (unstable) & \textbf{326--329 (stable)} & $\sim$20\% \textbf{faster} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

While the working set fits in cache, prefetch is pure overhead. Once it exceeds the L3
(at $2048^3$ three matrices total 48\,MB against a 12\,MB L3), demand misses reach DRAM,
the hardware prefetcher loses stream history under eviction pressure, and the constant
software lookahead genuinely hides latency: $\sim$20\% faster \emph{and} the large
run-to-run variance collapses. Taken together, the two experiments say: \emph{software
prefetch is a substitute for locality, not an addition to it}. A kernel that already has
locality (blocking + packing) gains nothing at any size; a kernel that lacks it gains
exactly where the hardware gives up.

SIMD            & \perfSimdInsns & \perfSimdLoneDmiss & \perfSimdLtwoMiss & \perfSimdLLCmiss & \perfSimdIPC \\
Prefetch (next\_B, T0, d=128)  & -- & \pfNextBTzeroDonetwentyeightTtwentyfourLoneDmiss & \pfNextBTzeroDonetwentyeightTtwentyfourLtwoMiss & \pfNextBTzeroDonetwentyeightTtwentyfourLLCmiss & -- \\
SIMD + Blocking & \perfOptimizedInsns & \perfOptimizedLoneDmiss & \perfOptimizedLtwoMiss & \perfOptimizedLLCmiss & \perfOptimizedIPC \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}%
}
\end{table}

Key observations at $1024$:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item The scalar prefetch kernel (next\_B, T0, distance 128, measured with HW prefetchers off) shows similar L1-D and L2 miss counts to the naive kernel, confirming that the scalar kernel is compute-bound and software prefetch adds negligible benefit even without hardware assistance.
    \item SIMD reduces instruction count dramatically (by ${\sim}4{\times}$) because each vector instruction processes 8 floats. This is the primary source of speedup at cache-resident sizes.
    \item The SIMD + Blocking kernel has the lowest cache misses thanks to MC${\times}$NC blocking, \emph{and} the lowest instruction count thanks to SIMD, achieving both benefits simultaneously.
\end{itemize}

The counters reveal the kernel's transition from compute-bound to memory-bound as the
matrix grows:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{IPC drops from 3.50 to 2.43} as size increases from 128 to 2048. At small
          sizes, the packed B panel fits in L2 and the FMA pipeline is nearly fully utilized.
          At 2048, L2 misses reach 3.5B and stall cycles dominate.
    \item \textbf{L2 misses jump sharply at 768} (from 1.5M to 113M), marking the point where
          the packed B panel ($K \times \text{NC} = 768 \times 64 = 192$ KiB) begins to exceed the
          2 MiB L2 capacity together with the A sub-panel and output block.
    \item \textbf{LLC misses remain negligible up to 1024} ($<$80K), showing that L3 absorbs
          the L2 overflow. At 2048, LLC misses reach 16M, as the full working set
          ($2048 \times 64 \times 4 = 512$ KiB per panel, but accumulated across all panels)
          exceeds L3, explaining the slight GFLOP/s drop at that size.
    \item \textbf{Instruction count scales as $O(N^3)$} as expected, growing from 86M at 128
          to 322B at 2048.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Analysis: Synergy Between Techniques}

\textbf{Note:} speedup numbers are not directly comparable across techniques because each benchmark run produces its own naive baseline (run-to-run variance in naive is ${\sim}2$--$4{\times}$ GFLOP/s).
The GFLOP/s column is the reliable cross-technique comparison.

\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{GFLOP/s by technique across matrix sizes (higher is better)}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrr}
\toprule
Size & Naive & SIMD (AVX2) & Prefetch (scalar) & SIMD + Blocking \\
\midrule
128  & \simdWidthNaiveOhtwentyeightGflops & \simdWidthAVXOhtwentyeightGflops & \pfNextBTzeroDonetwentyeightOhtwentyeightGflops & \optSweepOhtwentyeightGflops \\
256  & \simdWidthNaiveTwofiftysixGflops & \simdWidthAVXTwofiftysixGflops & \pfNextBTzeroDsixteenTwofiftysixGflops & \optSweepTwofiftysixGflops \\
512  & \simdWidthNaiveFtwelveGflops & \simdWidthAVXFtwelveGflops & \pfNextBTzeroDonetwentyeightFtwelveGflops & \optSweepFtwelveGflops \\
1024 & \simdWidthNaiveTtwentyfourGflops & \simdWidthAVXTtwentyfourGflops & \pfNextBTzeroDonetwentyeightTtwentyfourGflops & \optSweepTtwentyfourGflops \\
2048 & \simdWidthNaiveTfortyeightGflops & \simdWidthAVXTfortyeightGflops & \pfNoneNADNATfortyeightGflops & \optSweepTfortyeightGflops \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The three techniques target fundamentally different bottlenecks:

\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{SIMD (AVX2)} achieves \simdWidthAVXFtwelveGflops{} GFLOP/s at $512$ by processing 8 floats per FMA. At small sizes ($128$--$256$) where the working set fits in L2, SIMD-only is the fastest technique (\simdWidthAVXOhtwentyeightGflops{} GFLOP/s at $128$) because there is no cache-miss bottleneck and the B-packing overhead of the combined kernel is pure cost. At $2048$, it drops to \simdWidthAVXTfortyeightGflops{} GFLOP/s because the operands spill out of L2.

    \item \textbf{Prefetch (scalar)} provides negligible benefit: the best configuration achieves ${\sim}1.03$--$1.06{\times}$ speedup at all sizes. The scalar kernel is compute-bound, not memory-bound.

    \item \textbf{SIMD + Blocking} pays a fixed overhead for B-panel packing, which hurts at small sizes (\optSweepOhtwentyeightGflops{} GFLOP/s at $128$ vs.\ \simdWidthAVXOhtwentyeightGflops{} for SIMD-only). The crossover occurs around $512$, where the packing cost is amortized and the MC${\times}$NC blocking keeps the packed panel resident in L2. From $512$ onward, the combined kernel dominates: \optSweepFtwelveGflops{} GFLOP/s at $512$, \optSweepTtwentyfourGflops{} at $1024$, and \optSweepTfortyeightGflops{} at $2048$, while SIMD-only drops to \simdWidthAVXTfortyeightGflops{} at $2048$.

    \item The synergy is \emph{complementary}: SIMD removes the compute bottleneck (fewer instructions per FLOP); blocking removes the memory bottleneck (data stays in L2). Neither alone achieves both. The combined kernel sustains $>$100 GFLOP/s from $512$ through $2048$, while SIMD-only loses half its throughput at $2048$ and prefetch-only never exceeds the naive baseline by more than ${\sim}6\%$.
\end{itemize}
